projection.growthBasis: SIPRI estimates world military expenditure at USD 2.887 trillion in current US dollars for 2025, published April 2026. This latest completed-year estimate is held constant as an illustrative annual rate for the 2026 counter. No growth forecast is applied, and the counter is not a measurement of actual 2026 spending. Military expenditure includes more than expenditure on active wars.

source: SIPRI Trends in World Military Expenditure, 2025

sources.name: NCI Cancer Trends Progress Report — Financial Burden of Cancer Care (Mariotto et al. 2020)

categories.methodology: NCI annualized average cancer-attributable costs in the first year after diagnosis: USD 43,516.1 for medical services plus USD 1,873.9 for oral prescription drugs, totalling USD 45,390 in 2020 USD. Based on 2007–2013 US Medicare claims, averaging cancer sites and subtracting matched controls without cancer. This is an initial-care cost benchmark, not a complete treatment course, a cure, a global price or an inflation-adjusted 2026 quote.

sources.name: WHO — Global Technical Strategy for Malaria 2016–2030, 2021 update
WHO Africa — Bridging the funding gap to defeat malaria in Africa

categories.methodology: WHO's 2021 Global Technical Strategy estimated USD 10.3 billion of annual funding for malaria prevention, diagnosis, treatment and programme delivery by 2030. This is the total annual funding target, not the additional funding gap or the cost of global eradication. It excludes the separate estimated USD 0.85 billion per year for research and development. The strategy targets at least a 90% reduction in incidence and mortality by 2030, not eradication by 2050.

sources.name: Ceres2030 — Sustainable Solutions to End Hunger, Summary Report

categories.methodology: Ceres2030's 2020 model estimated average additional public spending of USD 33 billion per year through 2030: USD 14 billion from donors plus USD 19 billion from low- and middle-income governments. The scenario combines reducing hunger, doubling small-producer incomes and limiting agricultural emissions; it assumes coordinated interventions and induced private investment. This is a historical model benchmark, not a current funding quote or a guarantee that money alone ends hunger.

sources.name: World Bank — The Costs of Meeting the 2030 SDG Targets on Drinking Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene, Summary Report

categories.methodology: World Bank 2016 baseline estimate of USD 37.6 billion per year in 2015 prices for capital investment to extend safely managed drinking-water services to unserved populations in 140 countries during 2015–2030. This is the drinking-water component only; it excludes the additional ongoing operating and maintenance budget and is not an updated 2026 estimate.

sources.name: Sriudomporn et al. — Achieving Immunization Agenda 2030 coverage targets for 14 pathogens, Vaccine: X (2023 issue; online 2022)
Sriudomporn et al. — IA2030 cost study, full text (Europe PMC)

categories.methodology: Illustrative annual average of the study's USD 269.8 billion total in 2020 USD for 2021–2030, divided by 10 years: USD 26.98 billion. Covers vaccine products, routine delivery, and included campaigns and stockpiles for IA2030 coverage targets against 14 pathogens in 194 countries. It is the modelled total programme cost, not the incremental funding gap, universal vaccination of every child, or a verified 2026 budget. Costs and coverage vary by year and country.

sources.name: IRENA — Renewable Power Generation Costs in 2024

categories.methodology: Illustrative installed capital cost of 1 GW of utility-scale solar PV: 1,000,000 kW × USD 691/kW, IRENA's global weighted-average total installed cost for projects commissioned in 2024, in 2024 USD. This compares nameplate generating capacity; it does not include a complete electricity system, storage, continuing operations or a fixed number of homes powered. Local project costs vary.

sources.name: UN — Humanitarians launch USD 33 billion appeal for 2026 (8 December 2025)

categories.methodology: Approximately USD 33 billion requested in the December 2025 launch of the UN-coordinated Global Humanitarian Overview 2026, targeting 135 million people; USD 23 billion for 87 million people was identified as the immediate priority. This is a launch appeal budget, not the cost of meeting every humanitarian need or the remaining funding gap. Requirements and coverage may be revised during 2026.
